body.x: AIDIN ROBOTICS Inc. (CEOs Hyouk Ryeol Choi and Yoon Haeng Lee) participated on January 6 (local time) in the HUMANOID M.AX Alliance joint pavilion at CES 2026, a venue that offers a comprehensive view of “Korean-style humanoid” technologies.

AIDIN ROBOTICS is a startup founded in 2019 as a spin-off from Sungkyunkwan University’s Robotics Innovatory and is recognized for successfully localizing six-axis force and torque sensors for humanoid robots.

Building on this achievement, the company has expanded its portfolio of advanced sensors while broadening its business scope to include a range of robot modules and platforms. According to the company, all of these products are designed around AIDIN ROBOTICS’ proprietary force-sensing technology, delivering high reliability and stability.

At CES 2026, AIDIN ROBOTICS presented a comprehensive lineup of advanced force and torque sensors for humanoid robots. These sensors are designed to be mounted on humanoid robot hands, feet, and other joints to precisely detect force and torque, thereby maximizing the precision and delicacy of robotic motion.

The force-sensing technology that enables these capabilities combines multiple proprietary approaches, including detecting changes in electrode spacing and dielectric properties caused by pressure and deformation through capacitive measurement sensors, and intentionally controlling the spread of electric fields at electrode edges, known as the fringe effect, to enhance sensitivity.

body.cap: AIDIN ROBOTICS’ force and torque sensor lineup for humanoid robot joints and applications. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: In terms of sensitivity and stiffness, which are critical for robotic sensors, the company has achieved performance on par with or superior to traditional strain-gauge-based solutions, while also offering more competitive pricing than imported sensors.

Thanks to this balance of quality and cost competitiveness, AIDIN ROBOTICS’ sensors have reportedly received strong market responses. The wrist-mounted force and torque sensor AFT150 has been exported steadily to robotics companies and research institutions in 15 countries worldwide since its commercialization. In addition, the ankle-mounted three-axis force and torque sensor and the tactile sensor designed for integration into robot hands are scheduled for official launch in the first half of 2026, followed by domestic and overseas sales.

An AIDIN ROBOTICS representative said, “Robot hands equipped with our force and torque sensors can realize levels of delicate force control and contact points comparable to those of humans, enabling adaptive responses and tasks even with objects that have inherently low stiffness or durability. In particular, the version 2 prototype of our robot hand showcased at this CES integrates tactile sensors across the entire surface, allowing for a more compact design, and the response from visitors on site has been very positive.”

The representative added, “Leveraging the networks we established in North America and Europe through CES 2026, we plan to identify tangible customers and expand exports with products and technologies that meet their needs. As the global robotics market continues to grow rapidly, our goal is to proactively supply advanced sensor products, strengthen our presence in the humanoid sector, and evolve into a leading global provider of robotic sensing solutions.”

body.cap: AIDIN ROBOTICS demonstrates a robot hand equipped with its proprietary sensors. | Photo by AVING News

body.x: The HUMANOID M.AX Alliance is a public-private consultative body formed in April 2025 with the participation of 260 organizations and companies, including AI research institutes, robot manufacturers, component suppliers, and universities and research institutions. The alliance jointly promotes the demonstration and commercialization of AI-based humanoids in industrial environments. At CES 2026, the HUMANOID M.AX Alliance Pavilion went beyond simple product displays and presented a practical model for ecosystem building by connecting AI, platform, and component technologies.
